KEY MESSAGE 1...Cool and unsettled with lake enhanced showers 
gradually diminishing today.

A strong shortwave will dive southeast across the eastern Great 
Lakes early this morning, phasing with the closed low over the 
Canadian Maritimes by this afternoon. Forcing for ascent and deep 
moisture associated with the passing shortwave will continue to 
support a few areas of synoptically forced showers this morning, 
along with embedded areas of lake enhanced showers. Boundary layer 
flow will veer to the northwest through the morning hours, carrying 
the lake enhanced showers from east of the lakes before daybreak to 
southeast of the lakes after sunrise. The best coverage of showers 
will be found across Central NY and the Tug Hill region this 
morning, and also across the Chautauqua Ridge from upslope 
enhancement.

Deep moisture will quickly depart late morning through the 
afternoon, with a commensurate weakening of lake effect showers from 
west to east. Most areas should be dry by mid afternoon, with the 
exception of Central NY where a weak band of scattered showers may 
persist into this evening on WNW flow. A few spotty showers may 
continue this evening across Central NY, moving north across the Tug 
Hill region overnight as boundary layer flow backs to the west and 
eventually southwest. Otherwise, dry weather will prevail tonight 
for the rest of the area.

It will stay quite breezy today, with northwest winds gusting in the 
25 to 35 mph range. The strongest gusts will be along the lakeshores 
and the higher terrain of the Finger Lakes.

KEY MESSAGE 2...A few lake enhanced showers will continue Tuesday 
across the North Country, otherwise dry weather returns for the rest 
of the area.

Another fast moving mid level shortwave and associated surface low 
will race across Ontario and Quebec Tuesday in progressive WNW flow 
across southern Canada. Forcing for ascent from the passing 
shortwave and a modest increase in moisture will clip the North 
Country and Saint Lawrence Valley. This will combine with lingering 
lake induced instability to support a few showers across the North 
Country Tuesday through Tuesday evening. The most persistent showers 
will be found across the higher terrain of the Tug Hill Plateau and 
western foothills of the Adirondacks with an added boost of upslope 
flow.

Otherwise, the rest of the area will remain dry. Winds will increase 
again as a 30 to 40 knot low level jet crosses the eastern Great 
Lakes. This will support gusts of 20 to 30 mph areawide, and up to 
35 mph across the Niagara Frontier.

KEY MESSAGE 3...Colder and unsettled weather returns late in the 
week, with some wet snow potential mainly across higher terrain.

Forecast uncertainty abounds for late this week into next weekend 
with a wide spread in deterministic and ensemble guidance with 
respect to the strength and track of the late week system. 

A strong ridge will build across the Rockies during the second half 
of the week, forcing downstream height falls over the eastern CONUS, 
with a deep trough and broad mid level closed low established by 
Friday. A southern stream and northern stream shortwave will phase 
over the Ohio Valley by Thursday, allowing for a surface low to 
deepen with time. Height falls and DPVA from the approaching trough 
combined with moisture transport and frontogenesis ahead of the 
deepening low over the Ohio Valley will support increasing chances 
of rain from southwest to northeast on Thursday. Precip type should 
stay all rain through Thursday with colder air still displaced well 
north of the US/Canadian border.

The Ohio Valley low will give way to secondary coastal cyclogenesis 
along the Mid Atlantic coast by Thursday night, with the resulting 
coastal low moving northeast along or offshore of the New England 
coast Friday through Saturday. This phase of the system is highly 
uncertain, with some recent deterministic models and ensemble 
clusters showing a weaker and farther southeast track. 

In general, expect precipitation chances to continue Friday through 
Saturday, either from the system itself or from cool north/northeast 
upslope flow and a lake response. The airmass is not particularly 
cold, so higher terrain will have the best chance of changing over 
to wet snow, with precip type staying rain for much of the time 
across lower elevations until the coldest air aloft arrives Friday 
night through Saturday. NBM and LREF Grand Ensembles suggest a 30 to 
50 percent chance of 2 inches or more of snow accumulation across 
the highest terrain Friday through Saturday, but the probabilities 
of more significant 6 inch or greater amounts remains very low at 
less than 10 percent. 

The turn towards colder weather will be temporary, with strong 
ensemble support for a warming trend and return to above average 
temperatures later next week.
